title: Active lattice percolation: an apparently new universality class of percolation transitions
authors: Vernon M. Hughes, David A. Huse
abstract: We investigate a class of dynamic percolation models on a lattice, in which connections are added and removed by a set of local stochastic rules. In particular, the removal of any connection that can result in one connected cluster becoming two (or more) separate clusters is strictly forbidden. These models include and are inspired by a model for local quantum error correction for a toric code studied by Chirame, et al., PRX Quantum 6, 030363 (2025), who identified a phase transition with first-order characteristics, such as bistability and a discontinuous order parameter. We show numerically that this transition is a hybrid percolation transition (HPT), having characteristics of a continuous percolation transition such as diverging critical clusters while at the same transition having discontinuities like a first-order transition. We then modify this model to be fully isotropic, showing that the HPT remains. In both of these models, the steady state on one side of the HPT is an absorbing state; by turning on additional isotropic local stochastic moves, we remove the absorbing state and strongly suppress or remove the first-order transition, leaving an apparently continuous percolation transition. Curiously, the numerically-observed percolation critical exponents do not change significantly between the models with hybrid transitions and the model with an apparently continuous transition. These exponents are significantly different from known percolation transitions, indicating that this may be a new universality class.
summary: This work analyzes active lattice percolation models exhibiting complex phase transitions, identifying them as Hybrid Percolation Transitions (HPTs). By calculating critical exponents and comparing results across different model variations, the authors argue that these systems define a new universality class distinct from standard percolation theory. The research heavily relies on advanced Monte Carlo simulations to characterize the non-equilibrium critical behavior.
main_problem: The paper investigates dynamic percolation models to determine if the observed phase transitions belong to a novel universality class, particularly focusing on hybrid or apparently continuous transitions.
main_result: The critical exponents calculated for the active lattice percolation models are significantly different from known percolation transitions, suggesting the existence of a new universality class.
method:
The authors employ extensive numerical simulations (Monte Carlo) to calculate critical exponents ($	au, d_f, 
u$) and analyze the scaling behavior of order parameters ($ho$) near the transition point.
model_or_system: The system is a dynamic percolation model on a lattice where connections are added and removed stochastically, constrained by rules that forbid cluster splitting. Specific models include the local erasure flag model inspired by quantum error correction codes.
key_observables:
Steady-state flag density ($ho$), percolation critical exponents ($	au, d_f, 
u$), and the time required for the order parameter to cross a threshold.
important_parameters: The rate of stochastic moves ($\gamma$), the lattice geometry (honeycomb), and the initial state of the system ($p_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system reaches a steady state after a sufficiently long time, and that the observed exponents are robust across different model variations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the lattice dynamics (leaf/loop moves), the dependence of $ho$ on $\gamma$, the scaling of cluster size distributions ($n(s)$), and the convergence of fractal dimensions ($d_f$) for different model parameters.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first analyzing the original anisotropic model, identifying it as a Hybrid Percolation Transition (HPT). It then modifies the model to be isotropic, and finally, it analyzes the convergence of critical exponents across various parameter regimes to argue for a new universality class.
why_interesting: The study of non-equilibrium phase transitions in lattice models, especially those involving local constraints (like cluster preservation), provides a rich testing ground for generalized critical phenomena beyond standard equilibrium statistical mechanics.
